title: ESP32 WiFi + MQTT
description: Connect an ESP32 to WiFi and a public MQTT broker. The sketch publishes to its own topic and subscribes to it, so every message round-trips through broker.hivemq.com and toggles GPIO2 — a self-contained test of WiFi and MQTT with no external setup. Open the Serial Monitor at 115200 to watch it connect and exchange messages. The emulator advertises an open AP named "Velxio-GUEST".

title: Grove PAG7660: read a gesture (I2C)
description: Grove Smart IR Gesture Sensor (PAG7660) on I2C (0x68). Reads the gesture result registers the same way Seeed's Grove_Gesture library does and prints the gesture name. Open the sensor slider panel while running to pick a gesture (SDA=GPIO21, SCL=GPIO22).

title: HuskyLens: DFRobot's official I2C example (real library)
description: DFRobot's own HUSKYLENS_I2C.ino, byte for byte, running the vendor's real Arduino library against the emulated device: begin() knocks, request() pulls INFO+BLOCK frames in 16-byte I2C windows, and the serial monitor prints Block:xCenter=... exactly as on hardware. The library ships as extra sketch files (it is not in the Arduino index). Move the ID/X/Y sliders and the numbers follow.

title: HuskyLens: DFRobot's official UTILITIES example
description: The vendor's protocol torture test, ported from SoftwareSerial to I2C in three lines: it saves a screenshot AND a photo to the TF card (right-click the HuskyLens afterwards - both PNGs are in the SD panel), forgets, learns ID 1, names it TEST_NAME, writes and replaces custom texts on the screen, asks isPro and the firmware version, then prints Done. Watch the device screen while it runs - every step is visible.

title: HuskyLens: drive the screen — algorithms, learning, custom text
description: The sketch runs the device, and the device's own screen shows it: it cycles through the seven algorithms (watch the header change and Line Tracking swap the box for an arrow), learns the object as ID 2, names it, and writes custom text at coordinates — everything lands on the on-board display. Try the buttons too: the function button's edges dial the same algorithm menu, and holding the learning button forgets what the sketch taught.

title: HuskyLens: face-recognition door greeter
description: Face recognition as access control: learned face ID 1 gets a greeting and the green LED; any other ID is an unknown visitor and gets logged. Move the ID slider to 1 to be recognized, to 2-5 to knock as a stranger, and to 0 for an empty doorway.

title: HuskyLens: line-following steering signal
description: The line-tracking half of a robot, without the chassis: the line's X offset from the frame center becomes a signed steering command, printed as an ASCII gauge a motor mixer would consume. Sweep the X slider and watch the steering swing from hard left to hard right.

title: HuskyLens: pan servo follows the object
description: Camera-on-a-servo tracking: the object's X position (0-319) maps to the servo angle, so the pan head turns to keep the target centered. Move the X slider from edge to edge and the horn sweeps with it; the serial monitor prints the correction.

title: HuskyLens: photos and screenshots onto the TF card
description: The HuskyLens has its own TF card slot, and the protocol can use it: REQUEST_PHOTO saves what the camera sees, SAVE_SCREENSHOT saves the whole screen (UI included). The sketch shoots three of each; when it prints DONE, right-click the HuskyLens and open the SD Card panel - photo_0..2.png and screenshot_0..2.png are there, downloadable, and they travel with the project.

title: HuskyLens: read the detected object (I2C)
description: HuskyLens AI camera on I2C (0x32). Sends REQUEST_BLOCKS with the HUSKYLENS protocol and prints the detected object ID + center. Move the ID/X/Y sliders while running.

title: HuskyLens: UART mode (TX0/RX0)
description: The other interface: the HuskyLens wired to the ESP32's UART0 pins speaks the same protocol over serial at the port's own pace. The sketch sends REQUEST_BLOCKS as raw frames and parses the INFO+BLOCK answers from Serial. Fair warning, faithful to the hardware: the serial monitor shares this UART, so you will see the protocol's binary frames mixed with the sketch's prints - exactly what a logic analyzer on the real wires shows.

title: [STM32 + Arduino] GPIO Mirror
description: Cross-board demo: the STM32 Blue Pill toggles PA1 every 500 ms (wired to Arduino Uno pin 2). The Uno reads pin 2 and mirrors it to its built-in LED (pin 13). Shows heterogeneous multi-board simulation — QEMU STM32 driving an avr8js Arduino.

description: Cross-board UART: the STM32 Blue Pill sends a "PING n" message over USART1 (PA9 TX) into the Arduino Uno RX (pin 0). The Uno reads each line and blinks LED 13 + echoes "[Uno] got: ..." to its own Serial Monitor. Watch both monitors.

title: [STM32 + ESP32] GPIO Sync

title: [STM32 + STM32] Blue Pill → Black Pill

description: Blink the onboard PC13 LED and print to Serial on an STM32F103 Blue Pill (QEMU / libqemu-arm)

title: STM32 Blue Pill: SSD1306 OLED (4-pin I2C)
description: Drive the cheap 4-pin SSD1306 OLED module (GND/VCC/SCL/SDA) over I2C1 from an STM32 Blue Pill (SDA=PB7, SCL=PB6).

title: STM32 Serial Counter
description: STM32 Blue Pill prints an incrementing counter and uptime to Serial every second. Open the Serial Monitor to watch it. Onboard PC13 LED blinks as a heartbeat.

title: STM32: 7-Segment Counter
description: Count 0-9 on a 7-segment display driven by seven GPIO pins (PA0-PA6 = segments A-G) on the STM32 Blue Pill. Pure digital output: each digit pattern is written to the segment pins. Common-cathode (COM -> GND).

title: STM32: BMP280 Weather Sensor (I2C)
description: Read temperature and pressure from a BMP280 over I2C1 on an STM32 Blue Pill (SCL=PB6, SDA=PB7). The sensor runs as a QEMU I2C slave; values stream to the Serial Monitor. Demonstrates the STM32 hardware I2C master peripheral end to end.

title: STM32: DS1307 RTC Clock (I2C)
description: Read the current time and date from a DS1307 real-time clock over I2C1 on the STM32 Blue Pill (SCL=PB6, SDA=PB7). The QEMU DS1307 slave returns the live system clock in BCD, ticking once a second in the Serial Monitor.

title: STM32: MPU6050 IMU (I2C)

title: STM32: Push Button -> LED
description: Read a push button on PA0 (INPUT_PULLUP) and mirror it to the onboard PC13 LED on the STM32 Blue Pill. Pressing the button drives the GPIO input LOW; the firmware lights the LED while pressed. Demonstrates GPIO input injection.

title: STM32: RGB LED Color Cycle
description: Cycle an RGB LED through red, green and blue using three GPIO pins (PA0=R, PA1=G, PA2=B) on the STM32 Blue Pill. Pure digital output; common-cathode (COM -> GND).

title: STM32: Slide Switch -> LED
description: Read a slide switch on PA0 and reflect its position on the onboard PC13 LED of the STM32 Blue Pill. Flipping the switch drives the GPIO input HIGH/LOW. Demonstrates GPIO input injection from a latching element.

title: STM32: SSD1306 OLED Display (I2C)
description: Drive a 128x64 SSD1306 OLED over I2C1 from an STM32 Blue Pill (SCL=PB6, SDA=PB7). The framebuffer writes are captured by the QEMU I2C slave and rendered on the canvas. Shows "Hello Velxio!" with a live frame counter.

title: STM32: Stepper Motor
description: Rotate a stepper motor with the four-pin full-step sequence driven by GPIO pins (PA0-PA3) on the STM32 Blue Pill. Pure digital output: the firmware energizes coils A+, B+, A-, B- in order to step the rotor.

title: STM32: Weather Station (BMP280 + OLED)

Two LEDs blink along with each detection. Runs right away — no boot to wait for. Note that OpenCV is not available in Linux mode; the panel and the GPIO pins work there just the same.

description: Draws a filled screen, a rounded rectangle and text on a 320x240 ILI9341 TFT from an ESP32-S3 over hardware SPI (FSPI / GPSPI2).

title: BJT as a Switch
description: Base driven into saturation through Rb; collector pulled up via a load resistor. DC step input toggles Vce between ~0.2 V and Vcc.

title: BJT Common-Emitter Amplifier
description: Classic voltage amplifier: base biased by a divider, emitter degenerated by Re, collector resistor sets gain.

title: BJT Differential Pair
description: Long-tailed pair: a shared emitter tail resistor steers current between Q1 and Q2 according to the differential input.

title: BJT Emitter Follower
description: Common-collector buffer: unity voltage gain, high input impedance, low output impedance. Great as a driver stage.

title: Darlington Pair
description: Two cascaded NPNs multiply β — β_total ≈ β1·β2. Used when a single transistor can’t supply enough base current for a heavy load.

title: Diode Clamper (DC Restorer)
description: Series cap + parallel diode shifts the signal so its negative peak sits at 0 V. Output swings 0 → 2·Vpeak.

title: Diode Clipper
description: Two diodes to VCC/GND via a series resistor limit the output swing to roughly ±0.7 V — symmetric clipping.

title: Full-Wave Bridge Rectifier
description: Four diodes in a bridge rectify both halves of the AC input. Load R1 sees full-wave pulses at 2× the input frequency.

title: Half-Wave Rectifier
description: Single diode passes only the positive half-cycle of a 50 Hz sine. Load resistor drops the rectified voltage.

title: MOSFET Common-Source Amplifier
description: 2N7000 as a small-signal amp: drain resistor sets gain, source resistor stabilises bias. AC-coupled signal input.

title: MOSFET Low-Side Switch
description: 2N7000 NMOS with a pull-down gate resistor. Gate drive above Vth turns the device on and sinks current from the load to GND.

title: NPN Current Mirror
description: Reference current in Q1 is mirrored through Q2’s collector — matched transistors + shared Vbe make the collector currents equal.

title: Op-Amp Comparator
description: Open-loop op-amp compares V_in against a reference. Output saturates high when IN+ > IN-, low otherwise.

title: Op-Amp Integrator
description: Rf replaced by a cap: V_out = −(1/RC) ∫V_in dt. Square-wave in → triangle-wave out. Classic analog-computer building block.

title: Op-Amp Inverting Amplifier
description: Gain = −Rf/Rin. Rf = 10 k, Rin = 1 k → gain = −10. LM358 single-supply model clamps the output to [0, VCC−1.5].

title: Op-Amp Non-Inverting Amplifier
description: Gain = 1 + Rf/Rg. Rf = 10 k, Rg = 1 k → gain = +11. Output in-phase with input.

title: Op-Amp Schmitt Trigger
description: Positive feedback (R2 from OUT to IN+) adds hysteresis: two switching thresholds instead of one. Cleans up noisy signals.

title: Op-Amp Summing Amplifier
description: Virtual-ground summing junction: V_out = −Rf · (V1/R1 + V2/R2). Two-input mixer with unity gain per channel.

title: Op-Amp Voltage Follower
description: Unity-gain buffer: output tracks the non-inverting input exactly. Infinite input impedance, near-zero output impedance.

title: Parallel Resistors
description: Three resistors in parallel — total resistance is the reciprocal of the reciprocal sum. Ammeter shows total current.

title: PMOS High-Side Switch
description: P-channel MOSFET (IRF9540) sources current from VCC when the gate is pulled below VCC−|Vth|. Ideal for load switching.

title: RC High-Pass Filter
description: Swap the R and C of a low-pass and you get a high-pass. 1 kHz sine through C — R — GND.

title: RC Low-Pass Filter
description: 1 kHz sine through R = 1.6 kΩ and C = 100 nF. fc ≈ 1 kHz — output attenuated by −3 dB.

title: RL Low-Pass Filter
description: Inductor in series, resistor to ground. High frequencies dropped across L; low frequencies pass through.

title: Series Resistors
description: Three resistors in series carry the same current — ammeter reads V/(R1+R2+R3).

title: Series RLC Resonant Circuit
description: L = 1 mH, C = 1 µF gives fr ≈ 5 kHz. Sweep the signal generator — Vc peaks at resonance (Q-dependent).

title: Smoothed Half-Wave Rectifier
description: Half-wave rectifier followed by a 100 µF reservoir cap. Output is near-DC with ripple inversely proportional to C.

title: Voltage Divider
description: Two resistors divide a 5 V DC source in half. Classic first SPICE demo — expect 2.5 V across R2.

title: Voltage Doubler (Villard / Greinacher)
description: Two caps + two diodes extract roughly 2·Vpeak DC from an AC input. First stage clamps, second stage peak-detects.

title: Zener Shunt Regulator
description: Series resistor + reverse-biased zener clamps the output to Vz (5.1 V for a 1N4733) despite changing input.

title: 1-Bit ALU Slice (AND / OR / XOR / ADD)
description: A complete 1-bit ALU cell — AND, OR, XOR and ADD all computed in parallel, with a 4-to-1 MUX selecting which result drives Y. The carry path is wired so the slices cascade into a 32-bit ALU like in MIPS.

title: 1-Bit Magnitude Comparator
description: Three outputs decode the relationship between A and B: A>B, A=B, A<B. Built from two NOTs, two ANDs and one XNOR.

title: 2-Bit × 2-Bit Binary Multiplier
description: Four AND gates compute the partial products; two half adders sum the columns. The four output LEDs show the 4-bit product P3..P0 of two 2-bit numbers A1A0 × B1B0.

title: 2-Bit Equality Comparator
description: Two XNORs compare individual bits, an AND combines them. The LED lights only when A1A0 = B1B0.

title: 2-to-1 Multiplexer
description: Two AND gates feed an OR gate. SEL routes either D0 or D1 to Y. The textbook gate-level MUX.

title: 2-to-4 Line Decoder
description: Two select lines pick exactly one of four outputs. Each output is A·B for some combination of A/!A and B/!B. The backbone of address decoding inside every CPU.

title: 3-Bit Binary → Gray Converter
description: Two XORs convert a 3-bit binary input to its Gray-code form: G2=B2, G1=B2⊕B1, G0=B1⊕B0. Toggle the input switches and watch only one output flip per increment — the defining property of Gray code.

title: 3-Bit Gray → Binary Converter
description: Inverse of the binary-to-Gray converter — three input switches feed an XOR cascade running from MSB to LSB to recover the binary value.

title: 3-Input AND — All Three
description: Three slide switches drive a 3-input AND. The LED stays dark until every switch is HIGH at the same time.

title: 3-Input Majority Voter
description: Output is HIGH when at least 2 of 3 inputs are HIGH: Y = AB + AC + BC. Fault-tolerant logic in seven gates.

title: 3-to-8 Line Decoder
description: Three select bits drive eight outputs — exactly one LED lights at a time. The lit LED is the binary value of A2A1A0. Eight 3-input ANDs and three inverters.

title: 4-Bit Adder / Subtractor
description: A single mode line selects add (M=0) or subtract (M=1, via two-complement). Each B bit is XOR-ed with M and M also feeds the FA0 carry-in, so the same ripple chain computes A+B or A−B.

title: 4-Bit Carry-Lookahead Adder
description: Replaces the ripple chain with a parallel carry network. Generate / propagate signals + four lookahead expansions compute c1..c4 in constant gate-depth — the same O(log n) speedup pattern that scales to 64-bit CPU adders.

title: 4-Bit Magnitude Comparator
description: Compares two 4-bit numbers A and B. Four XNORs decide bit equality, a priority cascade of ANDs/ORs decides A>B, and a NOR derives A<B. Three LEDs decode the relationship live.

title: 4-Bit Parity Generator
description: Three cascaded XORs compute the even-parity bit of a 4-bit nibble. The LED is HIGH when an odd number of input switches are HIGH.

title: 4-Bit Population Count
description: Counts how many of four input switches are HIGH and outputs the count as a 3-bit binary number on three LEDs. Built as an adder tree — the same shape SIMD popcount instructions use in silicon.

title: 4-Bit Ripple Counter (T flip-flops)
description: Four T flip-flops chained into a ripple counter — impossible on the SPICE engine (no edge detection at DC). Each time you slide the CLOCK switch from LOW to HIGH the count advances; the four LEDs show it in binary, LSB at the top. The event-driven digital engine evaluates the flip-flops exactly. (Set ?digitalgates=off to see that ngspice cannot run this.)

title: 4-Bit Ripple-Carry Adder
description: Four full adders chained — A[3:0] + B[3:0] + Cin → S[3:0] + Cout. Toggle nine input switches to compute any 4-bit sum live. Twenty-six gates of pure combinational logic.

title: 4-Input AND Gate
description: Four switches feed a single 4-input AND gate. The LED lights only when every input is HIGH at once.

title: 4-to-1 Multiplexer
description: Two select lines route one of four data inputs to Y. Built from one 2-to-4 line decoder (the !A·!B...A·B combinations) feeding four ANDs into a 4-input OR.

title: 4:2 Compressor (Wallace Cell)
description: Five same-weight bits in, three out. Two cascaded full adders compress 5 bits into Sum + Carry + Cout in constant time — the building block of Wallace and Dadda tree multipliers.

title: 8-to-3 Priority Encoder
description: Eight input switches; three output LEDs encode the highest-numbered switch that is HIGH as a 3-bit binary number. A fourth "valid" LED lights whenever any input is active.

title: AND Gate — Both Switches
description: Two slide switches feed an AND gate. The LED lights only when both switches are HIGH.

title: AND Gate Alarm
description: Two arming switches feed an AND gate — the alarm LED lights ONLY when BOTH are ON (e.g. both doors closed). They are slide switches, so they latch: slide each one ON and it stays, so you can hold both at once. Pure logic, no MCU — runs on the digital gate engine.

title: AOI Gate (AND-OR-Invert)
description: A composite cell common inside CMOS libraries: two ANDs feed a NOR. Output = !((A·B) + (C·D)). Faster than three discrete gates in real silicon.

title: BCD → 7-Seg: Segment "a"
description: Lights segment "a" for digits 0,2,3,5,6,7,8,9 and leaves it dark for 1 and 4. One slice of a 7447-style decoder, gate-built so the K-map minimisation a = B3 + B1 + B2·B0 + !B2·!B0 is visible end-to-end.

title: BCD Validity Detector
description: Lights an LED only when the 4-bit input is a valid BCD digit (0–9). The complement (10–15) is detected by B3·B2 + B3·B1 and inverted to drive the "valid" lamp.

title: Buffer From Three Inverters
description: Three NOT gates in series invert three times → effectively a non-inverting buffer with three gate delays. Used for fan-out or to "regenerate" a weak signal.

title: Full Adder (Gate Level)
description: Three inputs — A, B and Cin — feed two XORs, two ANDs and one OR. The XORs give SUM, the OR of the ANDs gives Cout. Classic cascade-able adder cell.

title: Galaksija — 1983 Z80 home computer
description: A real 1983 Yugoslav home computer (Voja Antonić, public-domain ROM) built from discrete chips on the bus: a Z80 CPU runs its BASIC ROM, an inverter decodes the address map, a 64K RAM holds memory and renders the text screen from its own video RAM, and a memory-mapped keyboard feeds keystrokes. Click Resume, then click the canvas and TYPE — it boots to "READY" and you can enter Galaksija BASIC, just like the real machine.

title: Half Adder
description: XOR gives the SUM, AND gives the CARRY of two 1-bit numbers A and B. Two LEDs decode the result in real time.

title: Half Adder — NAND Only
description: A half adder built entirely from six 2-input NAND gates: four for the XOR sum, two for the AND carry. Proof that NAND alone is functionally complete.

title: Half Subtractor
description: Computes A − B for two 1-bit numbers. DIFF = A XOR B, BORROW = !A · B. The complement of the half adder.

title: Hamming (7,4) Encoder
description: Four data bits in, seven coded bits out. Three parity bits computed by XOR triplets implement the classic single-error-correcting code that protects ECC RAM and aerospace memory.

title: Intel 8080 Button Counter
description: A self-contained Intel 8080 chip running a 34-byte ROM. Press the INC button to count up in binary on 8 LEDs, press the RST button to clear. The CPU, RAM, and program are all inside the single chip on the canvas.

title: Kill the Bit (1975)
description: Dean McDaniel's iconic 1975 Altair 8800 reflex game, running on a programmable Intel 8080 chip with NO Arduino — powered by a regulated bench supply. A single LED walks across 8 LEDs; press the matching button at the right moment to kill it. The ROM is killbits.s (the chip's editable program); click Run.

title: NAND Gate — Universal
description: NAND is HIGH unless every input is HIGH. The LED stays on except when both switches are HIGH together.

title: NOR Gate — Idle Lamp
description: NOR outputs HIGH only when every input is LOW. The LED stays on while both switches sit at LOW.

title: NOT Gate Inverter
description: A slide switch drives a NOT gate. The LED is normally lit and turns off when the switch is HIGH.

title: OR Gate — Any Switch
description: Two slide switches into an OR gate. The LED lights as soon as either switch is HIGH.

title: XNOR — Equality Lamp
description: XNOR outputs HIGH only when both inputs match. A live equality detector — the LED stays lit whenever the two switches share state.

title: XOR — Difference Detector
description: XOR fires only when its inputs differ. Flip just one switch — the LED lights. Flip both back to the same — it goes dark.

title: XOR Built From NAND Only
description: Four 2-input NAND gates form an XOR. Proof that NAND is functionally complete — you can build every gate with just NANDs.

title: Z80 Comet Scanner
description: A faster, TWO-LED "comet" sweeps across 8 LEDs on a programmable Z80 chip — a brighter twist on the single-bit Larson. Written in Z80 assembly (scanner.s), NO Arduino: the chip runs standalone on a regulated supply. Click Run.

title: Z80 Larson Scanner (no board)
description: The programmable Z80 chip drives 8 LEDs with NO Arduino — powered by a regulated bench supply. Velxio runs custom chips as a general-purpose electronics simulator. Click Run: a single LED walks back and forth.

title: Z80 LED Chaser in C (no board)
description: A programmable Z80 chip walks a single LED back and forth, Larson-style — but the program is written in C (chaser.c) and compiled to the Z80 by SDCC. No Arduino: the chip runs standalone, powered by a regulated supply. Click Run. Requires sdcc on the backend.

title: ESP32-C6: Blink LED
description: Blink an external LED on GPIO8 of the ESP32-C6-DevKitC-1 (the same pin that drives the on-board WS2812 RGB LED).

title: ESP32-C6: SSD1306 OLED Display
description: Display text on a 128x64 SSD1306 OLED over I2C from the ESP32-C6 (default Wire pins SDA=GPIO23, SCL=GPIO22).

title: M5 Cardputer ADV - button (official example)
description: M5Stack's own BtnA test, unmodified: the G0 button on the top rail. Press it on the emulated board and the screen says Pressed, release it and it says Released, with a short beep either way. The shortest proof that the on-board button, the display and the speaker all answer.

title: M5 Cardputer ADV - buzzer (official example)
description: M5Stack's own speaker test, unmodified: alternates a 10 kHz and a 4 kHz tone once a second through the I2S speaker. Turn your volume up - the emulator plays the samples the guest actually writes.

title: M5 Cardputer ADV - display (official example)
description: M5Stack's own display test, unmodified: random coloured rectangles and text scattered across the 240x135 ST7789 panel, forever. A quick way to see the LCD path running at full tilt.

title: M5 Cardputer ADV - IR NEC send (official example)
description: M5Stack's own infrared test, unmodified: sends NEC address 0x1111 with a rising command over the IR diode on G44. Infrared is invisible, so the board flashes a violet dot with the decoded address and command each time a frame goes out.

title: M5 Cardputer ADV - microSD (official example)
description: M5Stack's own microSD test, unmodified: mounts the card on CS 12, lists the root, then creates, writes, appends, reads, renames and deletes files, finishing with a read/write throughput run. The card is a real FAT image you can load your own files into from the SD Card panel.

title: M5 Cardputer ADV - multi key press (official example)
description: M5Stack's own multi-key test, unmodified: shows every key held at once, joined with +. The TCA8418 controller reports up to three at a time, exactly as the hardware does.

title: M5 Cardputer ADV - REPL guessing game (official example)
description: M5Stack's own REPL demo, unmodified, across its three source files: a scrolling console with a prompt where you guess a number and it answers higher or lower. The richest of the official examples - keyboard, sprite rendering and a command loop together.

title: M5 Cardputer ADV - single key press (official example)
description: M5Stack's own keyboard test, unmodified: watches for the 'a' key and says so on screen. Click the key on the emulated keyboard, or focus the board and press it on your own keyboard.

title: M5 Cardputer ADV - text input (official example)
description: M5Stack's own text-entry test, unmodified: type a line, Backspace edits it, Enter commits it to a scrolling sprite above the prompt. Exercises the keyboard, the modifier keys and an off-screen canvas in one go.

title: M5 Cardputer ADV — Brick Blaster (juego con sonido)
description: A whole game on the board alone: no wiring, no microSD. The 240x135 LCD draws through an off-screen sprite so nothing tears, the 56-key keyboard steers the paddle, and the speaker carries the game — each brick row is a note of a pentatonic scale, so clearing a row walks up the scale and you can hear how you are doing without looking at the score. Where the ball lands on the paddle sets its angle, which makes it a game about aiming rather than reacting.

title: M5 Cardputer ADV — hardware tour (display, keyboard, microSD, IMU, LED, battery, mic)
description: A six-page diagnostic that drives every part of the board at once: a full-screen double-buffered sprite, the 56-key keyboard, the microSD card holding your project files, the BMI270 accelerometer with a live tilt bubble, the RGB LED, the battery gauge and the microphone as a live level meter. Press Tab to change page, arrows to move, Enter to act. Reach for this one when you want to see what the emulated hardware really does.

title: M5 Cardputer ADV — LCD + keyboard echo
description: The all-in-one M5Cardputer ADV (ESP32-S3): draw to the built-in 1.14-inch ST7789 LCD with M5GFX and echo whatever you type on the 56-key keyboard. Self-contained board, no wiring — press keys on the emulated keyboard and they appear on screen.

title: M5 Cardputer ADV — text terminal (official M5Stack example)
description: M5Stack's own inputText example, unmodified: type a line, press Enter, and it scrolls up into the log above. Exercises far more of the board than a plain print — an off-screen M5Canvas sprite, a vector font, scrolling text, and the Enter/Backspace keys — so it is the example to reach for when checking that the LCD and the 56-key keyboard both work end to end.

title: M5Stack Core - Button (official example)
description: Press A, B or C and the letter prints on screen; holding B for 700 ms clears it. The three front buttons, exactly as the vendor demos them. Ported from the official M5Stack example to M5Unified - the classic M5Stack library needs arduino-esp32 2.x and no longer compiles on the 3.x core, in the Arduino IDE too.

title: M5Stack Core - Display (official example)
description: Background colour sweep, text, rectangles, circles and triangles, then random triangles forever - the vendor's own tour of the LCD. Ported from the official M5Stack example to M5Unified - the classic M5Stack library needs arduino-esp32 2.x and no longer compiles on the 3.x core, in the Arduino IDE too.

title: M5Stack Core - HelloWorld (official example)
description: The canonical first sketch: Hello World on the 320x240 ILI9342C panel. Ported from the official M5Stack example to M5Unified - the classic M5Stack library needs arduino-esp32 2.x and no longer compiles on the 3.x core, in the Arduino IDE too.

title: M5Stack Core - Speaker (official example)
description: A beeps at 661 Hz for 200 ms, B holds a 112 Hz tone, C stops it. Speaker notes play through your computer at the sketch's real pitch. Ported from the official M5Stack example to M5Unified - the classic M5Stack library needs arduino-esp32 2.x and no longer compiles on the 3.x core, in the Arduino IDE too.

title: M5Stack Core - TFCard (official example)
description: Mounts the TF card on CS 4, checks for hello.txt, writes it, reads it back onto the screen. The card is a real FAT image you can load files into from the SD Card panel. Ported from the official M5Stack example to M5Unified - the classic M5Stack library needs arduino-esp32 2.x and no longer compiles on the 3.x core, in the Arduino IDE too.

title: M5Stack Core — built-in microSD + LCD
description: Read the M5Stack Core Basic's built-in microSD card (CS=GPIO4, shared VSPI bus with the LCD) and list its files on the built-in 320x240 screen. The card is emulated automatically — Velxio auto-copies your workspace files onto it — so no wiring and no card component needed.

title: M5Stack Core — button piano (speaker)
description: The three front buttons as a tiny instrument: BtnA/B/C each play a note on the built-in GPIO25 speaker (heard through your computer) while the LCD shows which key is down. Hold a button and the note holds; a self-contained board, no wiring.

title: M5Stack Core — Hello LCD + Buttons
description: The all-in-one M5Stack Core Basic (ESP32): draw to the built-in 2\" ILI9342 LCD with M5.Lcd and read the three front buttons (BtnA/B/C) with M5Unified — a self-contained board, no wiring needed. Press the buttons to change the on-screen counter.

title: M5Stack Core — LCD (Adafruit_ILI9341)
description: Drive the M5Stack Core Basic's built-in 320x240 LCD with the lightweight Adafruit_ILI9341 library (the Core's ILI9342C is 9341-compatible), read the three front buttons, and beep the built-in speaker (GPIO25) on each press. A self-contained ESP32 board — screen, buttons and speaker on-board, no wiring.

title: Netduino 2 Serial Counter
description: Netduino 2 (STM32F205, Cortex-M3) prints an incrementing counter over Serial. GPIO/LED support arrives once the F205 SoC is wired; serial works today under QEMU.

title: Netduino Plus 2 Blink
description: Blink the onboard PA10 LED and print to Serial on a Netduino Plus 2 (STM32F405, Cortex-M4) under QEMU.

title: Olimex STM32-H405 Blink
description: Blink the onboard PC12 status LED and print to Serial on an Olimex STM32-H405 (STM32F405RG, Cortex-M4) under QEMU.

title: Pimoroni Badger 2350 — BadgeOS factory firmware
description: Boot the badge's REAL factory firmware: press Run and BadgeOS v2.0.2 (ARM MicroPython + custom C modules) boots in the browser — the factory menu renders on the e-paper and is navigable with A/B/C/UP/DOWN. The full MicroPython source tree from github.com/pimoroni/badger2350 (main.py, and every app under firmware/apps - badge, clock, gallery, hydrate, list, the_compendium raycaster game, weather) is loaded as browsable folders in the file explorer for reference (binary assets omitted).

title: Pimoroni Badger 2350 — e-paper badge
description: The Badger 2350 comes alive: the 2.7" e-paper (SSD1680, 264x176) draws a name badge, A/B/C switch between badge, clock (real PCF85063A RTC at 0x51) and info screens, and UP/DOWN turn the rear case lights on and off. Everything runs on the in-browser RP2350 RISC-V emulator - click the buttons on the board.

title: Pimoroni Badger 2350 — hydration counter (partial refresh)
description: Water-intake counter inspired by the official BadgeOS hydrate app: A adds a glass, B removes one, C resets, and the case lights fill with your progress toward 8 glasses. Only the counter band is re-uploaded to the SSD1680 (partial RAM-window writes with per-row counter re-seek), so the header stays put between refreshes.

title: Pimoroni Badger 2350 — I2C scanner on e-paper
description: The e-paper draws a live I2C bus scan: every device Velxio attaches (temp sensor 0x48, EEPROM 0x50, PCF85063A RTC 0x51, DS1307 0x68) listed with its address, the EEPROM write/read self-test result and the current RTC time. Press A on the board to re-scan. Runs on the in-browser RP2350 RISC-V emulator.

title: Pimoroni Badger 2350 — MicroPython REPL
description: The Badger 2350 boots vanilla RP2350 ARM MicroPython (Cortex-M33) entirely in the browser, runs your main.py from its LittleFS and drops to a live REPL. This example prints a greeting and then a heartbeat with the front-button states (A/B/C/UP/DOWN) once a second - click the buttons on the board and open the Serial Monitor to watch. Switch the language selector to MicroPython to edit the .py.

title: Pimoroni Badger 2350 — RTC alarm clock
description: A big e-paper clock driven by the real PCF85063A registers: press A to arm the RTC alarm 10 seconds ahead (BCD alarm registers + AIE). When the chip fires it pulls the INT line (GPIO13) low - the screen flips to ALARM and all four case lights turn on. C clears the alarm flag and returns to the clock.

title: Pimoroni Badger 2350 — to-do list
description: A checklist on the e-paper like the official BadgeOS list app: move the cursor with UP/DOWN, tick the highlighted task with A (B clears all, C ticks all). Completed tasks get a filled checkbox and a strike-through, and the rear case lights fill up with your progress. Click the buttons on the board.

title: Pimoroni Galactic Unicorn — GPIO heartbeat
description: The Pimoroni Galactic Unicorn (RP2350, RISC-V) runs a GPIO heartbeat: it toggles GP2 and counts loops on Serial1 (GP0). A minimal self-contained sketch that shows the RP2350 RISC-V core booting and running timed GPIO/serial in the browser. Open the Serial Monitor to watch the counter.

title: Pimoroni Pico Plus 2 W — Blink + Serial
description: The Pimoroni Pico Plus 2 W (RP2350, RISC-V) blinks an external LED on GP2 and prints "blink" on Serial1 (GP0). Proves the RP2350 RISC-V core, GPIO output and delay()/UART all run in the browser emulator. Open the Serial Monitor to watch the log.

title: STM32 Black Pill (F401) Blink
description: Blink the onboard PC13 LED and print to Serial on an STM32F401CE Black Pill (Cortex-M4) under QEMU.

title: STM32 Blue Pill (F103CB) Blink
description: Blink the onboard PC13 LED and print to Serial on an STM32F103CB Blue Pill (Cortex-M3, 128KB flash) under QEMU.

title: STM32F4 Discovery LED Blink
description: Blink the onboard PD12 green LED and print to Serial on an STM32F4 Discovery (STM32F407VG, Cortex-M4) under QEMU.

title: UNIHIKER M10: AI voice-controlled light
description: DFRobot's advanced wiki project, verbatim: the Gravity DF2301Q offline voice sensor reports command IDs over I2C (103/104) and the script switches the LED on Gravity port P24. Press Run, then enable the mic on the sensor and say "Hello robot" to wake it followed by "Turn on the light" — or click the phrase buttons if your browser has no speech recognition.

title: UNIHIKER M10: blink an LED on edge pin 2
description: DFRobot UNIHIKER M10 boots Linux and blinks an LED on edge connector pin 2. Just press Run: the board boots Linux, the script uploads itself and starts.

title: UNIHIKER M10: buttons A/B + buzzer
description: Press the on-board A button (left edge of the board) to beep the buzzer and update the screen; B plays the POWER_UP melody. Uses pinpong.extension.unihiker like the official wiki tutorials. Just press Run and then click the A/B buttons on the board.

title: UNIHIKER M10: digital piano
description: The wiki's 'digital piano' basic example: eight touch keys on the screen, each one a note on the on-board buzzer. Press Run, then play the keys with the mouse (turn your sound on).

title: UNIHIKER M10: emoticon master
description: The wiki's 'emoticon master' basic example: the built-in emoji set on the screen. Tap the on-screen button (or the board's A button) to change the face.

title: UNIHIKER M10: Hello on the built-in screen
description: DFRobot's official 'Hello, UNIHIKER!' intro: draws colored text and a winking emoji on the built-in 2.8" screen with the unihiker GUI library. Just press Run: the board boots Linux, the script uploads itself and starts.

title: UNIHIKER M10: IoT smart home (SIoT)
description: The wiki's advanced IoT project: temperature and humidity published to SIoT topics, and a lamp switched by a subscription. The wiki wires two boards through a broker on the LAN; here the siot client loops back on this board, so publish -> subscribe -> act runs the same code without a second machine. Press Run and tap open / close.

title: UNIHIKER M10: servo motor control
description: The wiki's 'Servo Motor Control' intermediate example, verbatim: four on-screen buttons drive a 180 deg servo on Gravity port P21 (10 / 90 / 170 deg and a sweep). Press Run, then tap the buttons on the board's screen.

title: UNIHIKER M10: starry sky (touch the screen)
description: The wiki's 'starry sky' basic example: a galaxy background with an onclick handler — every tap on the screen adds a star where you pressed. Press Run, then tap the board's screen.

title: UNIHIKER M10: system clock on the screen
description: The wiki's 'system time' basic example: draws the date and a ticking clock on the built-in 2.8" screen with draw_digit, refreshed once a second. Press Run.

title: UNIHIKER M10: temperature and humidity monitor
description: The wiki's smart-home monitor, verbatim: a DHT sensor on port P21 shown on the screen, with the on-board buzzer alarming over 32 C. Press Run and drag the sensor's Temperature slider past 32.

title: UNIHIKER M10: traffic light on edge pads 0/1/2
description: DFRobot UNIHIKER M10 runs a red/yellow/green traffic-light state machine on its three micro:bit edge pads. Just press Run: the board boots Linux, the script uploads itself and starts.

title: UNIHIKER M10: ultrasonic range finder
description: The wiki's 'Ultrasonic Range Finder' intermediate example, verbatim: a Gravity URM09 on port P21 drives a vehicle distance monitor — under 10 cm the car on screen brakes. Press Run and drag the sensor's Distance slider.

title: Grove Smart IR Gesture over SPI (flip the DIP)
description: The same sensor, the other bus. Slide the 4-way DIP to all-ON and the chip leaves I2C for SPI exactly as the hardware does — the model follows it, so this sketch talks to the same registers through SPI.transfer(): address byte with bit 7 set to read, and a burst that auto-increments. CS is socket D3, the pad Seeed's own example uses. Flip the DIP back to I2C while it runs and the sketch stops getting answers, because the chip is no longer there.

title: Grove Smart IR Gesture: a XIAO on the socket, no wires
description: The Grove Smart IR Gesture Sensor is a XIAO carrier: seat a XIAO on its socket (drag it off and back to feel the magnet) and the I2C bus is made by the header itself, exactly like the hardware. The sketch reads the PAG7661QN gesture processor at 0x68 the way Seeed's driver does and names the gesture. Pick one in the sensor slider panel; flip the 4-way DIP to SPI or USB and the board says the chip is no longer on I2C, because it is not.

title: Grove Smart IR Gesture: read the actual IR image
description: The chip is a camera, not just a gesture oracle: besides the result it keeps the frame itself, and I2C can read it. This sketch does the datasheet's dance — lock the frame buffer, spin on the read-back, burst-read the pixels from the data port at 0x0F, unlock — and prints the image as ASCII in the serial monitor. Turn the board's camera on (click the lens) and you are looking at your own webcam through the sensor's eyes, one frozen frame at a time.

title: Grove Smart IR Gesture: thumb mode (and the tuning registers)
description: Seeed ships a thumb-mode example, and the chip really does change what it reports: write 2 to R_Gesture_Mode and swipes, fingers and pinches all go quiet — only thumb up and thumb down come back. This sketch also walks the tuning registers the hardware exposes: the IR illuminator (0x69), sensor gain and exposure (0x67/0x68), and MaxDetectDist (0x6D), which is a minimum brightness — wind it down and a hand that is too dim or too far stops being seen at all, camera included.

title: ReSpeaker Lite: buttons and the XU316 control bus
description: The board's own wiring, no audio involved: the MUTE and USR buttons reach the seated XIAO through the socket (active-LOW, exactly as the hardware wires them), and the XU316 answers on I2C 0x42. The sketch reports every button edge, cross-checks MUTE against the mute status the control bus publishes (0xF1/0x81), and reads the firmware version at boot. Click the buttons on the board while it runs.

title: ReSpeaker Lite: far-field mic level meter (I2S)
description: A XIAO ESP32-C6 seated on the reSpeaker Lite socket (drag it off and back to feel the magnet) reads the mic array over I2S (16 kHz, 16-bit stereo) and prints a live VU meter, RMS and peak to the serial monitor, plus the VNR and mute status from the XU316 I2C control surface at 0x42. Drive the mic level and tone from the control panel; click MUTE on the board and the meter drops to silence while the red LED lights — the I2C status follows.

title: ReSpeaker Lite: play a melody through your speakers
description: The reSpeaker drives a speaker on the real board, so in the simulator it plays through YOUR computer: a XIAO ESP32-C6 seated on the socket writes notes to I2S and the browser sounds them, with the board's playback meter lighting as it goes. Nothing is wired to the speaker connector because nothing should be — plugging the real board into a speaker is exactly what this models. Press Run and turn your volume up.

title: ReSpeaker Lite: track the talker (DOA + VNR over I2C)
description: The XU316's processing, watched from the sketch: a XIAO ESP32-C6 seated on the socket polls the control surface at 0x42 and prints where the talker stands (direction of arrival), how clean the voice is (VNR) and which algorithms are running. Move the Talker angle slider and the needle follows while VNR falls off-beam; switch beamforming or noise suppression off in the panel and watch the numbers tell you what each one was buying. DOA and the algorithm flags are Velxio-extension registers — the shipping firmware exposes VNR and mute only.

title: XIAO ESP32C6: Blink
description: Blink an external LED on D2 (GPIO2) of the Seeed Studio XIAO ESP32C6 - IDF v5.5 compile, in-browser esp32c6js engine.

title: Round Display: analogue clock (GC9A01 + RTC)
description: The shield as it is meant to be used: a XIAO ESP32S3 draws an analogue face on the 1.28 inch GC9A01 and takes the time from the PCF8563 on the same board, so the clock keeps its own time instead of counting millis(). The pins are Seeed's own (CS=D1 DC=D3 BL=D6 SCK=D8 MOSI=D10), written as raw GPIO numbers so the sketch says what it means. Note the backlight: drive D6 low and the glass goes dark, exactly as the hardware does.

title: Round Display: battery gauge (ETA3410 divider)
description: The shield's battery path, end to end: the v1.1 board reads the pack through a 100k/100k divider into A0 when the KE switch sits on the battery side, so analogReadMilliVolts(A0) x 2 IS the pack voltage - Seeed's own recipe. The sketch draws a round gauge on the GC9A01 and follows the Battery slider in the shield's control panel; flip the KE switch slider to 0 and the gauge honestly reports there is nothing to measure.

title: Round Display: files on the microSD (TF slot)
description: The shield's TF slot is a real FAT card in the simulator: the project's data files are auto-copied onto it, and clicking the shield opens an SD Card panel where you upload your own (images, audio, data). This example ships saludo.txt already on the card; the sketch mounts the slot (same SPI bus as the glass, CS=D2), lists the root and paints the file on the round glass.

title: XIAO ESP32S3 Sense: camera photos to microSD
description: The Sense as a camera: esp_camera_init runs the real esp32-camera driver (SCCB probe, LCD_CAM + DMA), then the sketch shoots three JPEG photos from your webcam and saves them onto the onboard microSD. Turn the Camera button on to shoot - then right-click the board and open the SD panel: the photos are listed under Card contents and can be downloaded.

title: XIAO ESP32S3 Sense: Hello
description: Serial hello-world on the Seeed Studio XIAO ESP32S3 Sense (in-browser esp32s3js engine - the camera, PDM mic and microSD examples build on this).

title: XIAO ESP32S3 Sense: onboard microSD
description: The Sense expansion board's TF slot as a real FAT card: the project data files are auto-copied onto it (source files stay off the card), and right-clicking the board opens an SD Card panel to upload your own (the card travels with the project). CS is GPIO21 on the shared SPI bus, exactly as Seeed wires it.

title: XIAO ESP32S3 Sense: PDM microphone level
description: The Sense's digital microphone over I2S PDM RX (clock GPIO42, data GPIO41, 16 kHz mono - Seeed's own wiring). Click the Mic button in the canvas toolbar to stream your computer's microphone; while it is off, a steady 440 Hz test tone keeps the level meter alive.

title: XIAO RP2040: Blink
description: Blink an external LED on D0 (GPIO26) of the Seeed Studio XIAO RP2040 - runs on the in-browser rp2040js engine.

title: XIAO RP2040: button cycles the on-board RGB
description: A pushbutton on D1 (GPIO27, active-LOW with the internal pull-up) steps the on-board user RGB LED through red, green, blue and off. Click the button while running - the LED is on the board, no LED wiring needed.

title: XIAO RP2040: on-board RGB LED
description: Cycle the Seeed Studio XIAO RP2040 on-board user RGB LED (red=GPIO17, green=GPIO16, blue=GPIO25, active-LOW). No wiring needed - the LED is on the board.

title: XIAO RP2040: traffic light
description: A three-LED traffic light on D0/D1/D2 (GPIO26/27/28) of the Seeed Studio XIAO RP2040: green, a yellow warning, red, and back - the classic sequencing exercise on the in-browser rp2040js engine.
